What problem do generics solve?

They move type errors from runtime to compile time, remove manual casts, and allow one algorithm to work across many types. Without them, collections hold Object, and a wrong element appears as a ClassCastException far from the mistake.
What is type erasure? Why did Java choose it?

The compiler checks generic types and then removes them: type parameters become their first bound or Object, casts are inserted at use sites, and bridge methods are added. It was chosen for migration compatibility: libraries could add generics in Java 5 without breaking existing binaries, and generic and non-generic code could interoperate. The cost is that type arguments are not available at runtime.
Predict the output. System.out.println(new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass());
true. There is a single runtime class, java.util.ArrayList.
Why is List<String> not a subtype of List<Object>, while String[] is a subtype of Object[]?

If the list assignment were legal, you could add an Integer through the List<Object> view and corrupt the list of strings. Arrays allow it (covariance) because they carry their element type at runtime and every store is checked, failing with ArrayStoreException. Erased generics have no such runtime check, so the compiler must reject it. Arrays' covariance is widely seen as a historical design flaw; it existed so that Arrays.sort(Object[]) could work before generics.
Explain PECS with an example.

Which lines compile? void b(List<? extends Number> l) { l.add(1); // A l.add(null); // B Number n = l.get(0); // C } void c(List<? super Integer> l) { l.add(1); // D Integer i = l.get(0);// E Object o = l.get(0); // F }

A fails. The list might be List<Double>. B works. null is a member of every reference type. C works. D works. Every possible list type can hold an Integer. E fails, because it might be a List<Object>. F works.
List<?> vs List<Object> vs raw List?

List<?> is a list of an unknown specific type: it accepts any list, you can only read Objects and add null, and it stays type safe. List<Object> accepts only a List<Object>, but you can add anything. Raw List disables checks completely. Prefer List<?> when you only need size() or to print elements.
What is a bridge method? Show when one is created.

A synthetic method generated by the compiler to preserve overriding after erasure. In class StringNode extends Node<String> overriding set(String), the parent's erased method is set(Object), so the compiler adds set(Object), which casts to String and calls set(String). It is also produced for covariant returns. Detect it with Method.isBridge() or javap -c. This is why a raw call with a wrong type fails with ClassCastException inside the subclass.
Why does this fail to compile? class A { void m(List<String> l) {} void m(List<Integer> l) {} }
error: name clash: m(List<Integer>) and m(List<String>) have the same erasure. Both become m(List), and a class cannot have two methods with the same JVM signature. Rename one.
Why does this fail? class Par implements Comparable<Par> { public int compareTo(Par p) { return 0; } } class Ch extends Par implements Comparable<Ch> { }

error: Comparable cannot be inherited with different arguments: <Ch> and <Par>. A class cannot implement a generic interface with two different type arguments, because they share one raw interface, and the bridge methods would conflict. Use a Comparator for Ch.
Can you create a generic array? How does ArrayList store elements?

new T[n] and new List<String>[n] are compile errors, since arrays need their runtime type for store checks. new List<?>[n] is allowed. ArrayList stores an Object[] elementData and casts on read. For a real T[], use Array.newInstance(Class, n). If you do (T[]) new Object[n], never expose the array: an outside caller gets a ClassCastException.

Predict the output. List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1)); List<String> s = (List) ints; System.out.println(s.size()); Object o = s.get(0); System.out.println(o); String t = s.get(0); System.out.println(t);

Prints 1, then 1, then throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String. The compiler adds a cast only where the String type is needed. Assigning to Object needs no cast, so the pollution stays hidden.
Does System.out.println(s.get(0)) throw for a polluted List<String> holding an Integer?

Yes. The compile-time type is String, so overload resolution chooses println(String), which requires a checkcast. Verified on Java 21. String concatenation "x" + s.get(0) also threw in the same test. If you first assign to Object, no cast happens.

Predict the output. static void p(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); } static void p(String o) { System.out.println("String"); } static <T> void call(T t) { p(t); } public static void main(String[] a) { call("s"); }
Object. Overloads are picked at compile time. In call, T is unbounded, and p(Object) is the only applicable choice. With <T extends String>, it prints String.
What is heap pollution? How can it occur, and how do you detect it?

A parameterized variable refers to an object of the wrong actual type. It arises from raw types, unchecked casts, and generic varargs. It does not fail at the pollution point, but at a later compiler-inserted cast. Detect: pay attention to unchecked warnings (build with -Xlint:unchecked, maybe -Werror), and use Collections.checkedList at the boundary with legacy code to catch the insertion.
What does @SafeVarargs do? Where can it be used?

It declares that a generic varargs method does not perform unsafe operations on its array, and it suppresses the warning at call sites. It is not verified by the compiler beyond placement. It is allowed on constructors, static methods, final instance methods, and private instance methods (Java 9+), since these cannot be overridden. A subclass override could otherwise make the promise false.
Predict the result. static <T> T[] arr(T... a) { return a; } static <T> T[] pick(T a, T b) { return arr(a, b); } String[] s = pick("a", "b");

ClassCastException. In pick the compiler does not know T, so the implicit varargs array is an Object[]. String[] s = … casts it to String[] and fails. Calling arr("a", "b") directly works, since there T is String and a String[] is created.
Can you instantiate T? List the alternatives.
Why can't static fields or static methods use the class's type parameter?

Statics belong to the single class, shared across all parameterizations. static T x would have to be both String and Integer. A static method can declare its own type parameter: static <U> Box<U> of(U u). Notice that Box<String>.staticMethod() is not valid syntax.
What is a reifiable type?

A type fully available at runtime: primitives, non-generic types, raw types, List<?>, and arrays of these. Non-reifiable: List<String>, T, List<? extends X>. Array creation needs a reifiable element type.
What is wildcard capture? Why does l.set(0, l.get(0)) fail on a List<?>?

The compiler treats each ? as a fresh unnamed type (CAP#1). l.get(0) returns it as Object, and set requires CAP#1, and Object does not convert to it. A private generic helper <T> void helper(List<T> l) gives the unknown type a name for the method's duration, so the call compiles.
Explain class Enum<E extends Enum<E>>.

It is a recursive bound that forces each enum to be parameterized by itself: Color extends Enum<Color>. So compareTo(E) accepts only the same enum, and EnumSet<E extends Enum<E>> can guarantee that it holds a real enum type. Without it, comparing Color with Size would compile.
Why is T extends Comparable<? super T> preferred over T extends Comparable<T>?

Some classes inherit compareTo from a parent. java.sql.Timestamp is a Comparable<Date>, and LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>. The stricter bound rejects them. Comparable consumes a T, so by PECS it should use super.
Why does Collections.max declare T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>?

Binary compatibility. The erasure of a type variable is its first bound. Listing Object first keeps the erased return type as Object, the same as before generics, so old compiled code still links. Without it, the method descriptor would return Comparable.
How can you get the generic type at runtime? What does Jackson's TypeReference do?

A value does not know its type arguments, but class declarations retain them in the Signature attribute. new TypeReference<List<User>>() {} creates an anonymous subclass whose declaration says "extends TypeReference<List<User>>". The constructor reads that through getClass().getGenericSuperclass(). Likewise, with reflection you can read a field's declared List<String> using Field.getGenericType().
Is catch (T e) allowed? What about throws T?

catch (T e) is not, since the handler is picked by runtime class. <X extends Throwable> void m() throws X is allowed, and is how Optional.orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X>) stays checked-aware. An unchecked cast in such a method makes a "sneaky throw" possible; see Exception Handling.
Does overriding work with generics? Will this override? class Base<T> { void put(T t) {} } class Sub extends Base<String> { void put(Object o) {} }

This is a name clash compile error. Sub.put(Object) has the same erasure as Base.put(T), but it does not override put(String), the parameterized form. Write void put(String s), and add @Override always, so the compiler confirms it.
What does this print? Static counter in a generic class. class Sp<T> { static int c = 0; Sp() { c++; } } new Sp<String>(); new Sp<Integer>(); System.out.println(Sp.c);
2. There is one class, so there is one static. C++ templates would produce two separate classes; Java does not.
What does var list = new ArrayList<>(); infer?
ArrayList<Object>. Nothing constrains the diamond. list.add(1); list.add("s"); compiles and prints [1, s], which is probably not what you meant.
What is the difference between a bounded type parameter and a bounded wildcard? When is each right?

<T extends Number> void m(List<T> a, List<T> b) names the type, so it can link parts of the signature: both lists have the same T, and a return value can be T. void m(List<? extends Number> a) is simpler if the type appears only once. Rule: if the type is mentioned once and only used for reading or writing, prefer a wildcard. If two places must agree, use a type parameter. A type parameter can have multiple bounds; a wildcard cannot. A wildcard can have a lower bound; a type parameter cannot.
Is generic code slower? Is there any runtime overhead?

Generics add no runtime types, so there is no per-parameterization code and no template bloat. Costs: a checkcast at reads (cheap, and usually eliminated by the JIT), and boxing, which is the real cost. List<Integer> stores references to heap objects, with worse memory use and cache locality than int[]. Use IntStream and primitive arrays on hot paths.
Write a generic method to find the maximum element of a list.
Write a generic, type-safe cache that stores different types per key.
What happens with the type parameter in class Box<T extends Comparable<T> & Serializable> after erasure?
T erases to Comparable, the first bound. Where the value is used as Serializable, the compiler adds a cast to it. List the bound you use most first, to reduce casts.
Why can't lambdas implement a generic method's functional interface?

If the single abstract method itself declares a type parameter, as in interface F { <T> T id(T t); }, there is no lambda syntax for type parameters, so a lambda cannot implement it. Method references can: F f = Main::identity;. Generic interfaces like Function<T, R> are fine, as T and R are fixed at the target type.
Design question: how do you design a generic Repository or Service base class in Spring?

Spring Data shows the pattern: interface CrudRepository<T, ID>. A concrete interface UserRepo extends JpaRepository<User, Long> fixes the type arguments in its declaration. Those arguments survive erasure in the class file, so Spring reads them by reflection (ResolvableType) to know the entity class. It also injects by generic type: @Autowired Repository<User, Long> r selects the matching bean.
A custom abstract service: abstract class CrudService<T, ID> with a constructor taking the repository. Avoid deep generic hierarchies; once a signature has three or more type parameters with bounds, composition usually reads better.
Why does List<Number> l = List.of(1, 2.0); compile, while List<Integer> a = List.of(1); List<Number> b = a; does not?

In the first, inference uses the target: E becomes Number, and 1 and 2.0 box and widen to Number. In the second, the list already has a fixed type, and invariance forbids the assignment. List<? extends Number> b = a; works.
What is the output of Comparator.class.getTypeParameters()[0], and how does reflection expose generics?

It prints T. java.lang.reflect.Type is the supertype of Class, ParameterizedType, TypeVariable, WildcardType and GenericArrayType. toGenericString() prints a full signature; Collections.class.getMethod("max", Collection.class).toGenericString() gives public static <T extends java.lang.Object & java.lang.Comparable<? super T>> T java.util.Collections.max(java.util.Collection<? extends T>).
Why is Map.get declared as get(Object key) instead of get(K key)?

A lookup cannot corrupt the map, so there is no type-safety reason to restrict it. The contract is based on equals, and objects of different types can be equal. For example, an ArrayList key can be found with an equal LinkedList. get(Object) also lets code holding a Map<?, V> perform lookups. It also predates generics and stayed this way for compatibility. The downside is that map.get(42) on a Map<String, V> compiles and silently returns null. IDEs and Error Prone flag this as a "suspicious call". The same reasoning applies to contains, remove and indexOf.
Can you write obj instanceof List<String>?

Only when it is provably safe. Since Java 16, instanceof with a parameterized type compiles if the static type of the expression makes the check exact, for example when coll is a Collection<String> and you test coll instanceof List<String> l. If obj is an Object, it is a compile error, because erasure means the JVM can only check List. Use obj instanceof List<?> l and then check or cast the elements one at a time.
What are the naming conventions for type parameters?

Single uppercase letters: T for a type, E for a collection element, K/V for map key and value, R for a result or return, N for a number, S, U and so on for second and third types, and ID is common in Spring Data (CrudRepository<T, ID>). Using single letters keeps type parameters visually distinct from real class names. If a name like Customer were used as a type parameter, it would shadow the real class.
Why should public methods avoid returning wildcard types like List<? extends Number>?

The wildcard passes the restriction on to every caller. They cannot add elements, they have to repeat the wildcard in their own variables, and type inference gets harder. Wildcards belong in parameters, where they make the method more flexible for callers. Return types should be concrete (List<Number>), or a type parameter of the method (<T extends Number> List<T>) when the caller decides the type. A rare exception is deliberately returning a read-only, covariant view.
What is a generic constructor? Does it relate to the class's type parameter?

A constructor can declare its own type parameters, independent of the class's: class Box { <T extends Number> Box(T seed) { ... } }. It is useful when the constructor needs a bound or relationship only during construction, for example <T extends Comparable<T>> Range(T lo, T hi), which stores derived values. A generic class can also have one: new <Integer>Pair<String>(1) is legal syntax, but the explicit form is almost never written because inference handles it. In practice, a static generic factory method is clearer.
Why does Stream.map take Function<? super T, ? extends R> rather than Function<T, R>?

So that more functions are accepted. With ? super T, a function written for a supertype works: a Function<Object, String> such as String::valueOf can map a Stream<Integer>. With ? extends R, a function returning Integer can be used where R is inferred as Number. With an invariant Function<T, R>, those calls would fail to compile even though they are type-safe. This is PECS applied to a function: it consumes T and produces R.
